title: Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve identification
subtitle: Find the trunk first, keep the capsule intact

sources.org: ENT UK and partner specialty associations (UK National Multidisciplinary Guidelines)
sources.title: Management of salivary gland tumours: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines (Sood S, McGurk M, Vaz F, J Laryngol Otol)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management in people aged 16 and over (NG36)

indications: Benign tumours of the superficial lobe, most commonly pleomorphic adenoma and Warthin tumour, after assessment with ultrasound and fine needle aspiration cytology or core biopsy.
Low-grade malignant tumours confined to the superficial lobe, as decided by the head and neck multidisciplinary team.
Diagnostic excision of a parotid mass when cytology is non-diagnostic and malignancy cannot be excluded.
Chronic recurrent parotitis or sialectasis failing conservative and endoscopic management (selected cases), and parotid metastases from cutaneous cancer as part of an MDT plan.
contraindications: A tumour arising in the deep lobe or a parapharyngeal extension that needs a different approach; image it properly first.
High-grade malignancy needing total parotidectomy, neck dissection or nerve sacrifice: this operation is then not the right one, and the MDT should decide the extent.
Lymphoma diagnosed on core biopsy, which is treated medically after diagnosis.
Medical unfitness, where a slow-growing benign tumour may reasonably be observed with the patient informed of the risks of growth and rare malignant change.
preparation: Ultrasound with fine needle aspiration cytology or ultrasound-guided core biopsy. MRI for deep lobe extension, suspected malignancy or a large tumour, as recommended in the UK salivary guideline.
Document facial nerve function before surgery with a recognised scale. Pre-operative weakness with a parotid mass suggests malignancy and changes the plan.
Discuss at the head and neck MDT where cytology or imaging suggests malignancy.

Consent risks to discuss: temporary facial weakness, which is common, and permanent weakness, which is less common; numbness of the ear lobe from great auricular nerve division; gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome); salivary collection or fistula; haematoma; a hollow below the ear and the scar; recurrence; first bite pain; and the possibility that the final histology shows a malignancy needing further treatment.
Plan facial nerve monitoring and confirm with the anaesthetist that no long-acting relaxant will be given after intubation.
positioning: Supine with a head ring and a shoulder roll, the head turned away from the operative side and extended moderately.
Reverse Trendelenburg tilt to reduce venous bleeding.
Tube fixed on the opposite side. Eye on the operated side lubricated and protected with a clear dressing so it can still be seen to twitch.
The whole half of the face, the ear and the upper neck in the field, under a clear drape or with the face exposed.
equipment: Facial nerve monitor and handheld stimulator.
Fine dissecting instruments: fine artery forceps (mosquito) for tunnelling over the nerve, fine scissors, bipolar diathermy at low setting, skin hooks, and loupes or a microscope if preferred.
Ties and fine absorbable sutures, suction drain.
Frozen section availability arranged in advance if a malignancy is possible.
anatomy: The parotid gland lies in front of the ear and over the masseter, wrapped by the parotid fascia. The facial nerve passes through it and divides the gland into a superficial and a deep part; this is a surgical, not an anatomical, plane.

The facial nerve leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen and enters the gland. Its trunk divides at the pes anserinus into temporofacial and cervicofacial divisions, then into the temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.

Landmarks for the trunk: the tragal pointer (the nerve lies deep and slightly anteroinferior to its tip), the tympanomastoid suture (the nerve lies deep to its medial end), and the posterior belly of digastric (the nerve lies at about the same depth, just above its attachment to the mastoid). The styloid process lies deep to the nerve.
The great auricular nerve crosses the sternocleidomastoid towards the ear lobe; its posterior branch can sometimes be preserved.

The retromandibular vein lies deep to the nerve branches within the gland and is a guide to the plane of the cervicofacial division. The marginal mandibular branch runs near the lower border of the mandible and crosses the facial vessels.
criticalSafety: Identify the facial nerve trunk using at least two landmarks before dividing any parotid tissue anterior to it.
Divide gland tissue only after the nerve has been seen deep to it: tunnel over the nerve, open the forceps, see the nerve, then cut.
Do not breach the capsule of a pleomorphic adenoma. Capsular rupture and spillage are the main cause of multifocal recurrence.

A functioning facial nerve is not sacrificed on an intra-operative impression alone. Sacrifice is a decision planned with the MDT and the patient, or taken only for gross tumour involvement with senior agreement.
structuresAtRisk: Facial nerve trunk and branches, especially the marginal mandibular and temporal branches
Retromandibular vein and external carotid branches
commonErrors: Looking for the nerve too superficially or too high, before the gland is fully mobilised off the cartilage and the digastric is seen.
Dividing gland tissue without first seeing the nerve beneath it.
Grasping the tumour to improve exposure and tearing the capsule.
Excessive bipolar near nerve branches, or traction on them, causing a neuropraxia.
Inadequate haemostasis under low blood pressure, leading to a haematoma that stretches the nerve.
complications: Temporary facial weakness, usually of one or more branches, and less commonly permanent weakness.
Ear lobe numbness, Frey syndrome, salivary fistula or sialocele, haematoma and wound infection.
Contour deformity, scar problems and first bite syndrome.
Recurrence of pleomorphic adenoma, often multifocal and years later, and unexpected malignancy on final histology.
postop: Document facial function in recovery and again once local anaesthetic effects have resolved.
Eye care if eye closure is incomplete: lubricants by day, ointment and taping at night, and early ophthalmology input for a significant weakness.
Remove the drain when output is low per unit protocol. Watch for a haematoma: increasing swelling and tightness under the flap needs urgent review.
Discuss the final histology at the MDT and with the patient. Arrange follow-up appropriate to the tumour type.

steps.emphasis: Facial weakness, Frey syndrome and ear lobe numbness discussed; mark the side; document whether nerve sacrifice has been discussed if malignancy is possible.
Cytology or core biopsy and imaging on display. For a presumed benign tumour, confirm the imaging shows a superficial lobe lesion.
Antibiotic per local policy for a clean head and neck operation; VTE prophylaxis by risk assessment.
Head turned away and extended moderately, reverse Trendelenburg, operated eye lubricated and protected but visible.
Ear, face to the lateral canthus and the corner of the mouth, and the upper neck in the field.
Retract by normal gland, never the tumour. Any capsular breach or spillage is irrigated, recorded, and reported to the MDT.
Bipolar on low power, away from nerve branches. Ask for a Valsalva manoeuvre to reveal venous bleeding.
Send the whole specimen; request frozen section only if the result will change what is done today.
Suction drain brought out away from the incision, layered closure. A sternocleidomastoid or SMAS flap may be used to fill the defect.
Record how the trunk was identified, which branches were dissected, whether the capsule was intact, and the great auricular nerve status.

step.parotid.incision-flap.title: Modified Blair incision and skin flap
step.parotid.incision-flap.why: The incision must give access to the trunk behind and the branches in front while staying in natural creases. The flap is raised superficial to the parotid fascia, which keeps the nerve branches deep and safe.
how: Incise in the preauricular crease, curve around the ear lobe towards the mastoid, then down into a skin crease in the upper neck, about two finger breadths below the angle of the mandible to stay clear of the marginal mandibular branch.
Raise the anterior skin flap in the plane just superficial to the parotid fascia, forwards to the anterior border of the gland, with skin hooks and traction-countertraction.
Keep the flap thickness even; do not go deep near the anterior border, where branches emerge from the gland.
structuresAtRisk: Facial nerve branches at the anterior border
pitfalls: Dissecting below the parotid fascia at the anterior border and dividing a branch as it emerges.
A thin, buttonholed flap that necroses or exposes the gland.

step.parotid.mobilise.title: Mobilise the gland posteriorly: great auricular nerve, sternocleidomastoid, cartilage, digastric
step.parotid.mobilise.why: The facial nerve trunk can only be found once the tail and back of the gland are freed from the sternocleidomastoid and the ear canal cartilage, and the posterior belly of digastric is seen. These are the landmarks that make the search safe.
how: Identify the great auricular nerve on the sternocleidomastoid. Preserve its posterior branch if the tumour allows; divide the anterior branch if it enters the gland.
Separate the parotid tail from the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, ligating the external jugular vein or its branches if necessary.
Free the gland from the cartilage of the external auditory canal down to the tragal pointer, with blunt dissection and bipolar on small vessels.
Find the posterior belly of digastric by following the anterior sternocleidomastoid border up to the mastoid, and expose its upper border.
pitfalls: Starting the deep search for the nerve before the digastric has been seen.
Using monopolar diathermy deep near the tragal pointer.

step.parotid.trunk.title: Identify the facial nerve trunk
step.parotid.trunk.why: Everything that follows is dissected from the trunk forwards. A trunk identified with confidence makes the rest of the operation a matter of following it; a trunk assumed rather than seen is how branches are cut.
how: Dissect bluntly in the plane between the cartilage and the posterior belly of digastric, spreading parallel to the expected course of the nerve and controlling small vessels with bipolar.

Use at least two landmarks: the trunk lies deep and slightly anteroinferior to the tragal pointer, deep to the medial end of the tympanomastoid suture, and at the depth of the upper border of the digastric.
Recognise the nerve as a white, cord-like structure running forwards and laterally. Confirm with the stimulator at a low setting before proceeding.
State aloud that the trunk has been identified and confirmed.
pitfalls: Mistaking a fibrous band or a vessel for the nerve; confirm by course, appearance and stimulation together.
Bleeding from the stylomastoid artery near the trunk treated with diathermy rather than pressure or careful bipolar.

step.parotid.nerve-dissection.title: Dissect along the nerve and lift off the superficial lobe
step.parotid.nerve-dissection.why: The superficial lobe is removed by following the nerve and its branches, dividing only the gland that lies superficial to them. Seeing the nerve before every cut is the whole technique.
how: Follow the trunk to the pes anserinus. Pass fine artery forceps along the superficial surface of the nerve, open them to lift the gland, look to confirm the nerve is deep, then divide the tissue between the blades.
Follow the division nearest the tumour last, so you work towards the tumour with the nerve already displayed.
Dissect each branch out to the anterior border of the gland as far as needed to remove the superficial lobe with the tumour and a cuff of normal gland.
Ligate the parotid duct where it leaves the gland and the vessels encountered. Keep bipolar away from the nerve, and avoid traction on the branches.
structuresAtRisk: Temporofacial and cervicofacial divisions and all five branches
pitfalls: Dividing tissue before the nerve has been seen deep to it.
Prolonged traction on a branch over the tumour, which causes a temporary weakness even when the nerve is intact.

step.parotid.trunk-bailout.title: Bail-out: the trunk cannot be found, or the nerve is involved
step.parotid.trunk-bailout.why: Some tumours sit over the trunk, and revision surgery distorts the landmarks. Persisting blindly in the wrong place is what injures the nerve; there are safer routes and the right moment to ask for help.
how: If the trunk cannot be found safely, call a senior and use a retrograde approach: find a peripheral branch, such as the marginal mandibular branch where it crosses the facial vessels or the buccal branch alongside the parotid duct, and follow it back.
Consider finding the nerve in the mastoid segment by drilling, if that expertise is available.

If the nerve appears involved by tumour, stop. A functioning nerve is not sacrificed without senior agreement and a prior discussion with the patient; send frozen section and plan with the MDT if necessary.
If a branch is divided, record it and repair it primarily with fine sutures under magnification, or with a cable graft, at the same sitting where possible.
pitfalls: Spreading deeper and deeper behind a large tumour without a landmark.
Sacrificing a functioning nerve on an unconfirmed impression of malignancy.

step.parotid.final-stimulation.title: Stimulate the nerve before closing
step.parotid.final-stimulation.why: A nerve that responds to stimulation at the trunk at the end of the operation is very likely to recover even if the face is weak afterwards. The result guides counselling and decisions the next day.
how: Stimulate the trunk at a low current and watch each branch territory, or the monitor channels, respond.
Stimulate any branch that did not respond, distal to the area of dissection, to localise the problem.
Record the result for the trunk and each branch in the note.
pitfalls: Not recording the stimulation result, so a weak face the next day cannot be interpreted.
Stimulating at a high current, which can spread and give a false reassuring response.
